transcript:
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
It reinforces our commitment to inclusive connectivity across our footprint. In November, our acquisition of a strategic stake in South Africa's fiber business, MAZIV, received ICASA's final approval. In fiber to the home, MAZIV's footprint exceeds 2.8 million homes, representing market leadership. The business also has scale in fiber to the business and fiber to the tower. With the injection of cash and assets from Vodacom, this transaction unlocks an opportunity to accelerate fiber deployment in South Africa and expand access to high-quality connectivity, particularly in historically underserviced communities.
In December, we announced an agreement to acquire an additional 20% stake in Safaricom. The acquisition, which is subject to certain conditions precedent and regulatory approvals, will result in the consolidation of Safaricom and cement the group's communication and fintech leadership in Africa.
For example, if we use our half-year numbers to September 2025 and extrapolate the combined revenues of Safaricom and Vodacom, we'll exceed ZAR 220 billion, with financial services making up 22% of service revenue. We remain on track to close this transformational deal in the current quarter. From a performance perspective, we delivered another excellent quarter. The group's commercial momentum and more stable macro backdrop gives us confidence in our medium-term growth trajectory and bodes well for the group's financial performance for our full-year results.
For Q3, at a group level, revenue was ZAR 43.9 billion, up 11%. Group service revenue grew 2.7% in rands and was up 13.6% on a normalized basis, tracking favorably against our medium-term targets. The quarter showcased another excellent performance from Egypt, with a stable performance in South Africa and further improvement in our international business.
I was particularly pleased with our performance in Beyond Mobile and, specifically, financial services. Beyond Mobile services reached 22.9% of group service revenue, up from 21.4% in Q3 of the prior year. Our financial service business, which is the largest component of Beyond Mobile, was up 24.7% in rands to ZAR 4.5 billion. On a normalized basis, financial service growth accelerated to 26.1%, with all our geographies improving from Q2. We remain Africa's leading financial services operator, with $501 billion of transactions processed through our mobile money platforms over the last 12 months, including Safaricom.
This represents an impressive $1.4 billion every day. Shifting focus to South Africa, service revenue grew 1.4% to ZAR 16.4 billion, supported by strong performance in the consumer contract segment and Beyond Mobile services.
Mobile contract revenue was 2.6%, and we expect our 1 February price ups to accelerate this trend into the final quarter. In prepaid, we left a strong comparison in the prior year and reported a decline of 3.6%. As mentioned, our Beyond Mobile numbers were good, with financial services up 8.4%, fixed up 7.9%, and some good project wins in IoT, pushing up IoT revenue by 33.9%. The revenue numbers for the quarter were not impacted by the MAZIV transaction. MAZIV is an associate and included in our books from 1 December 2025.
The transaction is not expected to have a material effect on the group's headline earnings for financial year 2026. Egypt delivered another excellent performance. In rand terms, Egypt's revenue was ZAR 11.1 billion and grew 43.7% in rands. Service revenue in local currency was up 39.7%, contributing 27.5% of the group result.
The growth was broad-based, with strong growth in consumer mobile, fixed business, and Vodafone Cash. Vodafone Cash revenue grew 59.4% to ZAR 926 million and increased its contribution to 9.7% of Egypt's service revenue. Financial service customers were up 28.9% to 13.5 million. For Q4, we expect service revenue growth to trend into the 20s as the business laps the 30% price increases from December 2024. Now, switching to our international business, the positive momentum continues. Reported service revenue was ZAR 8.8 billion, up 12.6%, making up 25.5% of the group.
Normalized service revenue was 15.4%, accelerating from the Q2 growth of 14.2%. The acceleration reflected an improvement in DRC and Mozambique. In DRC, we grew service revenue 16.3% in US dollars, supported by data and M-PESA.
Service revenue in Mozambique was up 7% in local currency, making a clear improvement from prior quarters. Tanzania continued to deliver excellent growth of 19.8% in shillings, while Lesotho was up 10.8%. M-PESA revenue was ZAR 2.6 billion, up 22.1%. Our fourth business segment is Safaricom. The results for the Safaricom group are disclosed on a biannual basis and therefore not included in the quarterly update. However, Safaricom did provide a market update on Ethiopia. The business is scaling at a good pace. Customers reached 12.2 million, up from 7.1 million a year ago.
Local currency service revenue growth in Ethiopia more than doubled. In December, we revised mobile data and voice pricing structures to support the long-term sustainability and quality of our services. The adjustments reflected evolving cost dynamics across the business, including continued investment in network expansion and modernization, as well as broader macroeconomic factors and currency movements.
This change to pricing structures follows constructive engagement with the government and regulator. That concludes my review. Raisibe and I are now ready to answer any questions you may have.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Thank you, Shamil. Our first few questions are from Prashendran of 36ONE. I'll take the first two of them, and then perhaps, Shamil, you can take the third one. The first question is just around the devices in South Africa, noting that 5G devices are up, growing nicely year-on-year. The question being, how many 3G and 2G devices do we still have on the network, and what are the trends there? I'll come back to that in a second.
The second question is, within the data traffic growth of 32.3%, is that for prepaid or postpaid or for both? And then the third question for you, Shamil, is, how much has voice revenue declined in the quarter in South Africa? So Prashendran, maybe just kicking off with the handset side of the question.
We've got still around 6 million 2G handsets on the network, but those are falling around 10% year-on-year at the moment. The biggest decline we're seeing across the base is on 3G. We're at about 2.4 million handsets now, and that's down around 40% year-on-year, clearly being compensated for by the 4G and 5G device growth. Then in terms of the data traffic question, actually, that 32% is reasonably even across both prepaid and contract, contract with slightly faster growth in the quarter.
But if we look at the quarter-on-quarter change from the last quarter to the Q3, the Q2 to the Q3, it's prepaid that really accelerated a bit. Shamil, to you on the voice revenue decline.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So the voice revenue decline is about -13% for the quarter.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Okay. Madhvi from HSBC.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Just to also specify that it's now about 30% of our service revenue.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Madhvi from HSBC has a number of questions, so if I can ask you to take out your pens and pencils. The first one is around the Safaricom stake and stake sale. He's asking about the prospects for the government's holding going forward, whether that could go to zero over time, and the potential that could have for an adverse regulatory climate. So what assurances do we have in place regarding government's continued investment in Safaricom?
The separate question on South Africa: Madhvi noting that with prepaid still weak, are we now seeing pressure in the contract side as well? So maybe a little bit of color around contract. And within prepaid, is the pressure really coming from WhatsApp bundles of Telkom and the competition from MVNOs? How should we think about that?
The final question, and I appreciate a lot from Madhvi, but they're also asked by several others, is just one on Egypt, is around sorry, is one around Egypt, and that's asking, are there any scope for price ups in Egypt in the short run?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Okay. So maybe firstly, on the Safaricom part, in terms of the government holding, I think government's very, very, very clear that they intend holding the 20% for the foreseeable future. And you don't need to take my word for it. You just need to look at the parliamentary transcripts on it. It's quite emotional for government even having sold down a percentage. But they see Safaricom as a strategic investment and have every intention of holding that for a very long time, if not forever.
Secondly, so on the second question on prepaid, is there contract pressure? No. So on contract, essentially, a little bit of, I would say, enterprise is flattish. Consumer is growing more than 5%, and that's why you've got a result of just over 2.6% for the contract segment. So contract continues to grow, consumer contract continues to grow strongly.
Enterprise has always got a little bit of pricing, and I think one of the big things there is not that we're losing customers. Customers are still growing. The big issue's been some of the legacy stuff. So I'll give an example. Universities now deciding to scale down on the bundles that they were giving students, that type of thing. So you'll get some of those things that people have exited, but a lot of that would be in the base going forward. In prepaid, where's the pressure coming from? I mentioned the -13% on voice. That's probably your biggest pressure point that you're faced with.
And then the data, revenue growth has not been as strong as we would have previously liked. The traffic is strong, but remember, we've gone through repricing, and that's where it's coming from.
We see Q4 being a lot stronger, and then going into the new year, we see that turning to positive. Then basically, in Egypt, in terms of price ups, we'll always strive for price ups, and we'll always have conversations around it. But I think it becomes price ups are more of an issue because the price floors and the regulated floor environment creates a very healthy growth. If there's a big currency movement, price ups become more important.
And in that context, as we've shown, the regulatory authorities are willing to consider and listen to that based on if inflation/currency has basically had a bigger movement, then they would be open up to they'd be open to those discussions.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
One small build on the business side of South Africa. So if you look at the overall Vodacom Business result, we are growing 6.7%. What we're doing well at the moment is where we're asking a little bit of pressure in mobile and at an account level. We're seeing good traction with our Beyond Mobile services, particularly areas like cloud, IoT, and fixed. Shifting gear to Jonathan from Prescient. He wanted a little bit of color around the competitive intensity or the competitive landscape in South African prepaid. Maybe you can just reiterate or clarify your point around the growth outlook.
He's just asking, when can we return to growth in prepaid? Separate to that, Jonathan's asking for some color around the drivers for the strong other service revenue line, which grew 23% in the quarter.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Okay. On prepaid, essentially, so firstly, big picture. From a competitive perspective, very much the same as Q3, except what we did was we repriced a lot of our bundles or what we call our LTE bundles to make sure that we were competitive. We took pricing from being below the line to above the line and provided customers with more clear, simple offers. And that's worked quite nicely for us. Of course, we were betting against a strong quarter last year because of the Two-Pot system and so on.
So when we look at the quarter-on-quarter performance and we look at all the different metrics, I think strong performance there. The residual issue, of course, is voice. And so basically, voice is under pressure, and we're trying to reduce the decline by offering things like unlimited voice and these type of things and bundles and so on.
But also, when you move from out-of-bundle to in-bundle, you see a temporary decline because you take that hit, but you've saved that revenue for longer. So those are kind of transformations that we're going. So we're busy with a, I'd say, there's a bit of a price transformation happening. We see that stepping down, the -3.6 being lower or much lower in Q4. And in Q1, we see it turning back into positive.
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
In terms of the question about the other services, so the main driver is IoT, but noting that those are contracts that in some cases are short-term and they're lumpy, but the main growth of the 23% was driven by that.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Nadim from Standard Bank is staying in South Africa, and I just wanted to know if the summer campaign met our expectations and any sense of what we thought actually worked well and what didn't in the period. Nadim, I see you had a question on the SA voice revenue decline in Q3. I think we've already nailed that one. So Shamil, maybe just a little bit on the summer campaign.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So, on the summer campaign, very much met our expectations. I mean, what we were trying to do is, of course, do some of the price transformation and offset it with the, let's say, increase in traffic, increase of utilization, increase of bundle purchases, and so on during the summer campaign, and rewarding that behavior with VodaBucks and so on. And then also, so we've seen that play out quite nicely during the quarter.
What we also wanted to do was more increase our direct purchasing on VodaPay and the number of users and so on on digital. And all of that has turned out very well, and we've exceeded our expectations in that regard. So we're quite happy with the performance that we're seeing.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Rohit from Citi, maybe this one's for you, Raisibe, the first one. Just wanted a bit of color around the South African EBITDA margin trend in the second half of the year and, I guess, calling out that previous guidance we had of around mid-single-digit growth in South Africa. Is that possible? He had a separate question then that I guess we can take between Shamil and myself around the data traffic growth in Egypt. What's driving that? And are you seeing higher data usage from 5G adoption in Egypt? But perhaps, Raisibe, you can kick off with the EBITDA.
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So we see EBITDA stable and a better outcome compared to the first half, in part as we have seen the revenue trends picking up, especially in the prepaid space, and also boosted by the price increase. Our cost efficiency programs continue, and we're quite confident that it will deliver. So that should create a stable margin, EBITDA margin, and also EBITDA growth.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
So on Egypt, what we're seeing is, of course, a 25% increase in traffic. So very happy with that. Coupled with an 8.9% growth in data customers. So that's helped to accelerate data revenue. What's driving it is investment. We see a payback of under a year when we basically put in new sites in Egypt. So it's driven by additional coverage on the one side, but mainly it's driven by additional 5G coverage that we've now launched. And given the high smartphone penetration in Egypt, that's picking up quite nicely.
But it's also alleviating pressure on the 4G network, which is then allowing us to monetize faster there. The other thing that we do very well in Egypt, which we've now basically taken as best practice across the group, is monitoring what we call the busy hour.
So normally, when you build a network, you build for you dimension the network for busy hour. We built a tool using AI that actually looks at multiple busy hours during the day and then determines and comes back with a recommendation on where you should build or put the CapEx first so that you get immediate monetization of that. And that's now playing out into the different markets, also rolling out into the IB markets and so on, and is helping to make sure that the CapEx spend is even more targeted to generate more revenue faster.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
We're going to move to questions from Jono from Absa. He has a few, so pens at the ready, please. First one around the dynamic between data revenue growth in South Africa, prepaid data revenue growth of 3%, and then the data traffic growth of around 30%. Are you going to keep the same level of promotional activity into Q4 and then into FY27? Second question around IoT. Is there scope for additional contract wins under the RT29 tender? So can this type of growth, I guess, continue?
Tanzania noting a slight slowdown quarter-over-quarter. Was this across both GSM and fintech or skewed to one side or the other? Or maybe just a little bit of color around why TZ slowed a little?
And then finally, around the Safaricom transaction, Jono is noting that the East African competition authorities have penciled in a submission date for 16 February. Given this is the biggest deal they've looked at, is there a risk they could delay the transaction approval into financial year 2027?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So maybe just to start off with on the data revenue growth. So effectively, what we're seeing is that, as you can see, the traffic growth has been very strong. Now, normally, we get a much better growth coming through in terms of the monetization than the 3% that you saw in the quarter. And the reason for that is the repricing that we went through in terms of taking stuff from below the line, making it more visible above the line. That helped us to grow customers.
It helped us to consolidate spend from various customers into single SIMs and so on. So we're quite happy with what it is. Of course, summer is summer, so when you step into the next phase, you don't run promotions continuously.
So yes, some of the promotions will step down, and then, of course, we'll run other lesser promotions that are not, let's call it, summer promotions. But you'll see, as that transformation happens and people are spending more, you'll also see that the data absolute revenue growth will accelerate. So that's what we're expecting, is that the data revenue growth, the traffic, we think will stay high, but we think we'll see a better monetization of the data growth as we were seeing before we went through this repricing, transparent stuff that we did.
And so I think let's just say we're quite happy that the strategy and the plan that we've put in place will work in terms of taking prepaid back to growth. The growth rates for next year, we're looking at just slightly above inflation-type growth for South Africa while we're doing that last bit of transformation.
The broader group will be within the targets that we've communicated in our growth targets in service revenue and EBITDA. In terms of IoT, yes, definitely more opportunities to win on RT29. We're seeing a lot of focus on people moving to prepaid electricity meters and so on. And also, the work that we've done in water and that we continue to do, work that we continue to do with our water tower and so on in the IoT segment is we're starting to get more and more wins in that respect, so we'll continue to push.
It can be, to Raisibe's point earlier, it can be a bit lumpy from time to time because it takes a while sometimes to win some of these. And then you've got the short-term revenue, and then you've got, of course, the ongoing part of that as well.
In Tanzania, the slowdown is very much to do with elections and the disruptions that happened in that market. You saw an entire market slowdown during that period. Once that period finished into December, you basically saw revenue growth accelerate back to the previous levels that we were experiencing. Then in terms of the approvals, we think, I mean, of course, things can take longer than you expect, but we don't see big delays in terms of the transaction. We're still hopeful that we'll be able to close it before the end of March.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
One quick follow-up from Jono before we move on to the next set of questions. I just wanted to know if there's any material or noticeable changes in the competitive environment in South Africa since we last spoke in November?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
No, not really. I mean, I'd say very much the same. We're seeing MVNOs come and go at a rapid pace, so that's been quite interesting. And some, I'm told, very, very little uptake. So that's been quite interesting. No big changes in pricing. Of course, everybody had their summer promos and their summer offers and so on, but I don't think there's been any massive changes. We've seen postpaid changes and postpaid price-ups from almost everyone, so that's gone through. And yeah, so not much more. No real aggression or anything of that sort.
And of course, I mean, one of the big things would be just kind of we've gone through that repricing part, which, as I said previously, was caused by some changes in pricing, not so much from the MVNOs but really, I would say, led by MTN.
But we've done our own transparent transformations and so on, and we've seen them stopping some of those promotions as well.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
You're going to shift to Myron from BofA. Perhaps the first question for you, Raisibe. He's asking around the Safaricom debt or I suspect this is around the acquisition debt, when it could become tax-deductible or if it could become tax-deductible. There is a clarification around the split between consumer and enterprise contract in South Africa, so I'll perhaps help with that in terms of revenues. Third one, Shamil, for you. Have the authorities now said no to further price-ups in Egypt? So have we got a definitive no?
And related to that, why would Egypt service revenue grow in the '20s in Q4 despite decent customer growth and data usage? The final question he has, again, perhaps for you, Shamil, is around the amount of prepaid revenue we're now being purchased through VodaPay. So Raisibe, to you on the Safaricom debt, acquisition debt?
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So the debt is non-tax-deductible, as in the term debt. The approach that we have taken is that we will look at opportunities for refinancing, as we have done previously with the Egypt transaction where we managed to refinance part of the bundle with the preferences. So the good thing is that we are already in discussions with the banks in terms of taking the first part of the Safaricom transaction into prefs. You'd appreciate the size of the transaction, that we can't go into preferences for the whole packet all in one go.
So we will start the process as we progress. The other angle is that for all our non-tax-deductible debt, we prioritize in terms of repayment. And previously, we did repay some of the debt. So that is the approach that we'll continue to take in this case.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
I'll take the revenue split in South Africa postpaid between consumer and enterprise. It's not quite 50/50. It is skewed to the contract segment, the consumer contract segment, excuse me. So to get the math to work, consumer contract, as Shamil said, growing 5% to 6%, and enterprise is in a small decline. That's how we square the circle there. Shamil, did you want to take the one around price-ups in Egypt?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So the price-ups in Egypt, effectively, there's no imminent price-up coming. But have they said no? No, they haven't said no. So essentially, it's a discussion that we always have, and you have to go with a motivation of the impact and how inflation has impacted you and these types of things. So let's just say you've got to have very good reasoning. I mean, if you're coming with a 3, 4, or 5% impact, they're not going to jump over the table and put a price up. So you need to it's got to be where it's really where let's say the inflationary pressures have affected the business or rather the industry.
So I mean, so that's where we are at the moment. Why 20%? Well, effectively, I mean, if you look at your traffic growth, why it's not 20%.
It's in the 20s, just to be clear. Basically, what that means, if you look at your traffic remember what I've always said? Traffic times rate. Rate is steady. Traffic converts into revenue. So previously, if you think about it, traffic, 25%, rate steady, you should have seen 25% growth, okay? Let's say you've got a few years. Example. Then if you put the price up on top of that, that's what took you to the 39% growth. So if you don't have that, traffic times rate will give you the growth rate for Egypt. So if your traffic is growing in the 20s, your revenue will grow in the 20s.
In terms of how much airtime is being purchased through VodaPay, we're at about 12%, and that's growing all the time. So it's notching up slowly.
Remember, we were at 3% for the better part of, sure, 10, 15 years. So actually, it's been very good in terms of, in the last year, 18 months, we've more than tripled the amount of airtime we're selling directly.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Prashendran from 36ONE has a follow-up. I can probably take this one. Let's see how it goes. With the massive transaction finalized on 1 December, how much fixed-line revenue in South Africa moved from the top line to the share of profits and associate? Because we are still reporting growth in South Africa. So Prashendran, there's no material impact on revenue. We still retain the relationship with the customer as effectively an ISP. What will obviously change is the margin profile of that revenue going forward as you move from the owner of the infrastructure to the reseller of that infrastructure.
Madhvi from HSBC had a follow-up. Shamil, how do we see the new data regulations in South Africa impacting Vodacom, both in terms of bundle expiry, and data transfer rules?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So on the data regulations, so firstly, I think the good part is that all the shorter-term bundles, which are about 80% of what the industry sells, are not affected. So that has been purely excluded. There are certain things that we're not happy with. The rollover on normal bundles, all of that, that's fine. The issue comes in specifically on FWA. So that part, we will go back to the, so the choices are simple. Put the price up to compensate, or they need to remove it.
So the regulators overstretch their hand a bit in terms of it because, as an example, they also look after broadcasting, but they don't tell MultiChoice what to include in their bundles. So that's the piece that we will have a discussion with them because it doesn't come into effect immediately.
So we will both as an industry and as Vodacom have a discussion with them in terms of the impacts of that and what does that mean. Because the last thing you want to do is to have to compensate by putting the price up. From the telco perspective, you'd have to do that to manage the impact and to make sure that it doesn't have a big impact on or a big impact on your numbers.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Anoop, yeah.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
But it's only for a small portion of basically the numbers. And that, we think, we'll have a conversation because I think you can't roll over a 500 GB bundle. It's a simple logic.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Anoop from Moon Capital had a question around the margin outlook for Egypt without further price increases. Raisibe, maybe that's one for you?
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. I mean, Egypt at half-year was roughly 44%. And that is the kind of level that we still expect. So although, I mean, the normal really bracket of 42, the levels where we are at 44 is still quite a strong margin, 46%. So that is still the level that you are comfortable with. But yeah, I mean, the absence of a price increase is not something that we are particularly concerned about. Egypt is still having some momentum to grow. And we expect that while service revenue will moderate, but inflation is also moderated, and therefore, their costs are well, well controlled. So they will still be able to maintain some margin.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
I've got a question from Robert of Deutsche Bank. He notes that the South African 10-year yield has continued to fall now to its lowest level in a decade, which is good news for all of us. Does this change how we think about our overall leverage profile? And is there any perhaps even anecdotal evidence of improving confidence for B2B customers with regard to new ICT projects in South Africa? So maybe, Raisibe, you can lead with that one. And then for Safaricom, just to clarify, Robert, just on the Safaricom deal, the approval process is moving along, and yes, we do expect at this point still to close in this calendar quarter, Q1.
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
So I mean, good macros definitely welcome, but we all know that these kind of things come and go. So what we have done now, we continue to pay off debt, prioritize on the basis of expensive debt, being how it is priced as well as non-tax deductibility, converting to prefs, and we'll continue that journey. Now, while the deleverage is part of our strategy, we have just currently taken new debt. We've done preferences to finance the massive acquisition, and we will soon also pick up the debt relating to the Safaricom transaction. So the basket keeps on changing, and our focus is optimization so that our overall cost of funding is controllable.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Anything to add on the B2B environment or South Africa more broadly?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. I think the more positivity we can get, exchange rates improving, and so on. We need to see that converting into stronger GDP growth. The outlook looks very positive. And so I think that will stand us in good stead as we go into the new year. So inflation is much lower than before. So I think we're going into a better environment, interest rates coming down. So yeah, the trajectory for South Africa looks a lot more positive, coming off the gray list, the upgrade in terms from the rating agencies. So I think all in all, a very positive outlook for SA going forward.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
A question from Jonathan of Prescient is asking around our strategy to convert those remaining 6 million 2G customers in South Africa to 4G or 5G handsets and avoid churn within the space. Obviously, Jonathan, just to note, within that 6 million, there will be a whack of IoT devices.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So look, I think there's a couple of things that we're doing. One is the industry is now making sure we can—we've got a clear recommendation from the industry forum to government, and we've been having long conversations with them about stopping the import of 2G devices outside of the IoT devices, 2G and 3G for that matter. We want to—actually, prioritizing 3G is even more important to us than the 2G part, but we have to move the 2G and 3G customers off. So what we've done is a couple of things.
Firstly, and you'll see that across the group in terms of the acceleration of—we've added more than 15 million data customers in the nine months to date this year. So we've beaten all our targets. And what we're doing is device financing, both ourselves and third parties.
So things like FoneYam from PEP, plus our own services, plus third-party services, all of that helps to basically reduce the number of 2G, 3G devices in the network. Secondly, price points. We're now at $25 a smartphone, but we've also got $15 cloud-based phones. Consumers are taking it up, but they prefer nicer phones.
